q-138965.name: Question 1
q-138965.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={t}^{2},\,y=t+1,\,t\in [0,2].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
q-138965.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(t+1)\sqrt{{(2t)}^{2}+{(1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(t+1)\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

q-138967.name: Question 2
q-138967.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={t}^{2}-1,\,y=\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t,\,t\in [1,2].
$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.
q-138967.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=1$ to ${t}_{2}=2.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)=2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t)={t}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\sqrt{{(2t)}^{2}+{({t}^{2}-1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+{t}^{4}-2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\sqrt{{t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, factoring the expression ${t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\sqrt{{t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\sqrt{{({t}^{2})}^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot {t}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\sqrt{{({t}^{2}+1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\cdot |{t}^{2}+1|\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{2}-1)\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using direct integration we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}({t}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi \cdot {[\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}-t]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2\pi [(\frac{{2}^{5}}{5}-2)-(\frac{{1}^{5}}{5}-1)] \\  & =2\pi [\frac{22}{5}+\frac{4}{5}] \\  & =2\pi \cdot \frac{26}{5} \\  & =\frac{52\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}

q-138970.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=3t-{t}^{3},\,y=3{t}^{2},\,t\in [0,1].
$$

Calculate the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis.
q-138970.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t-{t}^{3})=3-3{t}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})=6t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{{(3-3{t}^{2})}^{2}+{(6t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{9-18{t}^{2}+9{t}^{4}+36{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+18{t}^{2}+9}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, factoring the expression $9{t}^{4}+18{t}^{2}+9,$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+18{t}^{2}+9}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}\sqrt{9({t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}\cdot 3\sqrt{{t}^{4}+2{t}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\sqrt{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\cdot |{t}^{2}+1|\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}({t}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{4}+{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =18\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{4}+{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =18\pi \cdot {[\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}+\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =18\pi [(\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{3})-(\frac{0}{5}+\frac{0}{3})] \\  & =18\pi \cdot \frac{8}{15} \\  & =\frac{48\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-352091.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)]=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t), \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sec}⁡(t)+\operatorname{tan}⁡(t)|-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)]=\operatorname{sec}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{[-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)]}^{2}+{[\operatorname{sec}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)]}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-2+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-2+[{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)]}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the identity ${sin}^{2}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)=1$ and ${sec}^{2}⁡(t)-1={tan}^{2}⁡(t)$ we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-2+[{sin}^{2}⁡(t)+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)]}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-2+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡(t)-1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\sqrt{{tan}^{2}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot |\operatorname{tan}⁡(t)|\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi [-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)]_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =-2\pi [\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)] \\  & =-2\pi (\frac{1}{2}-1) \\  & =-2\pi \cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
